Ensemble smoothers: EnKS, EnsembleRTS, fixed-lag, square-root and IES

A filter is causal: its analysis at time ttt uses the observations up to ttt and no later ones. For a reanalysis, or any retrospective study, the object you want also uses the observations after ttt:

p(xt∣y1:T),t<T.p(\vect{x}_t \mid \vect{y}_{1:T}), \qquad t < T.p(xt​∣y1:T​),t<T.
(10.1)

An ensemble smoother gets there cheaply. It runs the filter once, stores the ensembles, and sweeps backward, recombining them with no adjoint and no extra runs of the model.

One regression organises the chapter. The backward step regresses the present on the future, using the members themselves as samples of the joint distribution. EnKS and EnsembleRTS are that step, FixedLagSmoother truncates it, and EnsembleSqrtSmoother keeps its mean and replaces its anomalies. The same two things make the regression fail in each case: too few members to estimate it, or a forecast that treats a wrong model as exact. IES closes the chapter, and it is a different method for a different problem, an iteration over one window with no backward pass.

The backward step¶

The linear-Gaussian recursion¶

Take xt+1=Fxt+ηt\vect{x}_{t+1} = \mat{F} \vect{x}_t + \gvect{\eta}_txt+1​=Fxt​+ηt​ with xt∈RDx\vect{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}xt​∈RDx​, F∈RDx×Dx\mat{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}F∈RDx​×Dx​ and ηt∼N(0,Ση)\gvect{\eta}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta)ηt​∼N(0,Ση​). Given y1:t\vect{y}_{1:t}y1:t​, the pair (xt,xt+1)(\vect{x}_t, \vect{x}_{t+1})(xt​,xt+1​) is jointly Gaussian, with cross-covariance Σx,t∣tF⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topΣx,t∣t​F⊤. Conditioning on xt+1\vect{x}_{t+1}xt+1​ gives the mean μx,t∣t+Gsmooth,t(xt+1−μx,t+1∣t)\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t} + \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} (\vect{x}_{t+1} - \gvect{\mu}_{x,t+1 \mid t})μx,t∣t​+Gsmooth,t​(xt+1​−μx,t+1∣t​), with the smoother gain

Gsmooth,t=Σx,t∣tF⊤Σx,t+1∣t−1∈RDx×Dx.\mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} \mat{F}^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid t}^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}.Gsmooth,t​=Σx,t∣t​F⊤Σx,t+1∣t−1​∈RDx​×Dx​.
(10.2)

Given xt+1\vect{x}_{t+1}xt+1​, the later observations say nothing more about xt\vect{x}_txt​, by the Markov property. Averaging over xt+1∣y1:T\vect{x}_{t+1} \mid \vect{y}_{1:T}xt+1​∣y1:T​ then gives the Rauch-Tung-Striebel recursion Rauch et al., 1965, which starts from the filter at t=Tt = Tt=T:

μx,t∣T=μx,t∣t+Gsmooth,t(μx,t+1∣T−μx,t+1∣t),\gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid T} = \gvect{\mu}_{x,t \mid t} + \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} \left(\gvect{\mu}_{x,t+1 \mid T} - \gvect{\mu}_{x,t+1 \mid t}\right),μx,t∣T​=μx,t∣t​+Gsmooth,t​(μx,t+1∣T​−μx,t+1∣t​),
(10.3)
Σx,t∣T=Σx,t∣t+Gsmooth,t(Σx,t+1∣T−Σx,t+1∣t)Gsmooth,t⊤.\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid T} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} + \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t} \left(\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid T} - \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t+1 \mid t}\right) \mat{G}_{\text{smooth},t}^\top.Σx,t∣T​=Σx,t∣t​+Gsmooth,t​(Σx,t+1∣T​−Σx,t+1∣t​)Gsmooth,t⊤​.
(10.4)

The smoothed covariance never exceeds the filtered one, since Σx,T∣T≤Σx,T∣T−1\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,T \mid T} \le \gmat{\Sigma}_{x,T \mid T-1}Σx,T∣T​≤Σx,T∣T−1​ starts the recursion and the difference stays negative semi-definite. Cosme et al. (2012) set out this family of linear-Gaussian solutions.

The same step on members¶

The filter stores two ensembles for each window, the analysis Xt∣t\mat{X}_{t \mid t}Xt∣t​ and the next forecast Xt+1∣t\mat{X}_{t+1 \mid t}Xt+1∣t​, each in RNE×Dx\mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_x}RNE​×Dx​. Member eee of the forecast was propagated from member eee of the analysis, so the two rows together are one sample of (xt,xt+1)(\vect{x}_t, \vect{x}_{t+1})(xt​,xt+1​). That correspondence is all the method relies on. Their sample cross-covariance estimates Σx,t∣tF⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topΣx,t∣t​F⊤ with no F\mat{F}F in sight, so the dynamics can be nonlinear and need no tangent. Write the anomalies as X~t∣t\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}X~t∣t​ and X~t+1∣t\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}X~t+1∣t​, and take the pseudo-inverse, because the forecast covariance has rank at most NE−1N_\mathcal{E} - 1NE​−1:

G^smooth,t=X~t∣t⊤X~t+1∣t(X~t+1∣t⊤X~t+1∣t)+.\hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t} = \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} \left(\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}\right)^{+}.G^smooth,t​=X~t∣t⊤​X~t+1∣t​(X~t+1∣t⊤​X~t+1∣t​)+.
(10.5)

Applying this to each member gives xt∣T(e)=xt∣t(e)+G^smooth,t(xt+1∣T(e)−xt+1∣t(e))\vect{x}_{t \mid T}^{(e)} = \vect{x}_{t \mid t}^{(e)} + \hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t} (\vect{x}_{t+1 \mid T}^{(e)} - \vect{x}_{t+1 \mid t}^{(e)})xt∣T(e)​=xt∣t(e)​+G^smooth,t​(xt+1∣T(e)​−xt+1∣t(e)​) Evensen & van Leeuwen, 2000. Stack the rows, and write Dt+1=Xt+1∣T−Xt+1∣t∈RNE×Dx\mat{D}_{t+1} = \mat{X}_{t+1 \mid T} - \mat{X}_{t+1 \mid t} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_x}Dt+1​=Xt+1∣T​−Xt+1∣t​∈RNE​×Dx​ for what smoothing changed about the future. The identity (A⊤A)+A⊤=A+(\mat{A}^\top \mat{A})^{+} \mat{A}^\top = \mat{A}^{+}(A⊤A)+A⊤=A+ then removes the square matrix altogether:

Xt∣T=Xt∣t+Dt+1X~t+1∣t+X~t∣t.\mat{X}_{t \mid T} = \mat{X}_{t \mid t} + \mat{D}_{t+1} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^{+} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}.Xt∣T​=Xt∣t​+Dt+1​X~t+1∣t+​X~t∣t​.
(10.6)

This is gaussx.ensemble_rts_step, whose docstring writes it as Xts=Xta+DF+AX_t^s = X_t^a + D F^{+} AXts​=Xta​+DF+A, with FFF the forecast anomalies and AAA the analysis anomalies. The recursion starts at the final window, where XT∣T\mat{X}_{T \mid T}XT∣T​ is the analysis, and no later data exist to change it.

The product is contracted through the smaller of NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ and DxD_xDx​, so no larger square matrix appears, and X~t+1∣t+\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^{+}X~t+1∣t+​ comes from a singular value decomposition. Singular values at or below a cutoff are dropped, by default NE+DxN_\mathcal{E} + \sqrt{D_x}NE​+Dx​​ times the machine epsilon relative to the largest. When NE≤DxN_\mathcal{E} \le D_xNE​≤Dx​, rounding always leaves one such value, because X~t+1∣t\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}X~t+1∣t​ annihilates the constant vector. A whole backward pass costs TTT of these decompositions, each O(NEDxmin⁡(NE,Dx))O(N_\mathcal{E} D_x \min(N_\mathcal{E}, D_x))O(NE​Dx​min(NE​,Dx​)). Going through singular values rather than X~X~⊤\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\topX~X~⊤ matters in float32, which Program 10.7 measures.

EnKS and EnsembleRTS are one algorithm¶

Read (10.6) as a Kalman update whose observation is the future, and it is the Ensemble Kalman Smoother. Read (10.5) as the RTS gain with its Σx,t∣tF⊤\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topΣx,t∣t​F⊤ estimated from members, and it is an ensemble RTS smoother Evensen, 2003. filterax ships both names over one function, so that code can say which reading it means. Both run a reversed jax.lax.scan.

No process noise: the step inverts the dynamics¶

Suppose the forecast carries no noise, so that Xt+1∣t=Xt∣tF⊤\mat{X}_{t+1 \mid t} = \mat{X}_{t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topXt+1∣t​=Xt∣t​F⊤ with an invertible F\mat{F}F, and suppose NE>DxN_\mathcal{E} > D_xNE​>Dx​ with a full-rank X~t∣t\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}X~t∣t​. Then X~t+1∣t=X~t∣tF⊤\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} = \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topX~t+1∣t​=X~t∣t​F⊤, so X~t+1∣t+=F−⊤X~t∣t+\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^{+} = \mat{F}^{-\top} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^{+}X~t+1∣t+​=F−⊤X~t∣t+​, and X~t∣t+X~t∣t=I\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^{+} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} = \mat{I}X~t∣t+​X~t∣t​=I. Putting this in (10.6), the analysis cancels:

Xt∣T=Xt∣t+(Xt+1∣T−Xt∣tF⊤)F−⊤=Xt+1∣TF−⊤.\mat{X}_{t \mid T} = \mat{X}_{t \mid t} + \left(\mat{X}_{t+1 \mid T} - \mat{X}_{t \mid t} \mat{F}^\top\right) \mat{F}^{-\top} = \mat{X}_{t+1 \mid T} \mat{F}^{-\top}.Xt∣T​=Xt∣t​+(Xt+1∣T​−Xt∣t​F⊤)F−⊤=Xt+1∣T​F−⊤.
(10.7)

So the whole smoothed trajectory is the final analysis run backward through F−1\mat{F}^{-1}F−1, and nothing else of the filter’s history survives. If the model is exact, that is correct: every state is a known function of the final one, and XT∣T\mat{X}_{T \mid T}XT∣T​ has all the data. If the truth has process noise, the backward run is wrong in two ways. It has no way to absorb what the model missed, and a damped F\mat{F}F has an F−1\mat{F}^{-1}F−1 that amplifies the final error at every step. Program 10.9 shows the identity and both outcomes. The exact smoother with Ση=0\gmat{\Sigma}_\eta = \mat{0}Ση​=0 reduces to the same thing through (10.2), and chapter 17 covers KalmanSmoother.

The square-root smoother¶

EnsembleSqrtSmoother is the backward analogue of the deterministic filters of chapters 6 and 7 Tippett et al., 2003. It takes the mean from (10.3) with the sample gain, and it replaces the member-wise anomalies with a symmetric transform of the analysis anomalies. Take V=(X~t+1∣tX~t+1∣t⊤)+X~t+1∣t∈RNE×Dx\mat{V} = (\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^\top)^{+} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_x}V=(X~t+1∣t​X~t+1∣t⊤​)+X~t+1∣t​∈RNE​×Dx​, so that G^smooth,t=X~t∣t⊤V\hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t} = \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^\top \mat{V}G^smooth,t​=X~t∣t⊤​V, and define

Ψ=I+V(X~t+1∣T⊤X~t+1∣T−X~t+1∣t⊤X~t+1∣t)V⊤,X~t∣T=Ψ1/2X~t∣t,\gmat{\Psi} = \mat{I} + \mat{V} \left(\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid T}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid T} - \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^\top \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}\right) \mat{V}^\top, \qquad \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid T} = \gmat{\Psi}^{1/2} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t},Ψ=I+V(X~t+1∣T⊤​X~t+1∣T​−X~t+1∣t⊤​X~t+1∣t​)V⊤,X~t∣T​=Ψ1/2X~t∣t​,
(10.8)

with Ψ∈RNE×NE\gmat{\Psi} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}}Ψ∈RNE​×NE​ and negative eigenvalues clamped to zero. The sample covariance of the result is X~t∣t⊤ΨX~t∣t/(NE−1)\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t}^\top \gmat{\Psi} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} / (N_\mathcal{E} - 1)X~t∣t⊤​ΨX~t∣t​/(NE​−1), and substituting gives exactly (10.4) on sample covariances. The constant vector is in the null space of V⊤\mat{V}^\topV⊤, so Ψ1/21=1\gmat{\Psi}^{1/2} \vect{1} = \vect{1}Ψ1/21=1, and the anomalies stay centred, by the argument of (6.6).

What differs from EnKS¶

The means agree, since both move by G^smooth,t\hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t}G^smooth,t​ times the mean of Dt+1\mat{D}_{t+1}Dt+1​. The anomalies need more care than “a rotation”. Split the analysis anomalies into their regression on the forecast and a residual, X~t∣t=X~t+1∣tG^smooth,t⊤+Rt\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} = \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} \hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t}^\top + \mat{R}_tX~t∣t​=X~t+1∣t​G^smooth,t⊤​+Rt​, with X~t+1∣t⊤Rt=0\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^\top \mat{R}_t = \mat{0}X~t+1∣t⊤​Rt​=0. (10.6) then gives the EnKS anomalies as

X~t∣T=X~t+1∣TG^smooth,t⊤+Rt.\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid T} = \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid T} \hat{\mat{G}}_{\text{smooth},t}^\top + \mat{R}_t.X~t∣T​=X~t+1∣T​G^smooth,t⊤​+Rt​.
(10.9)

Their sample covariance is (10.4) plus the cross terms between X~t+1∣T\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid T}X~t+1∣T​ and Rt\mat{R}_tRt​. With NE−1≤DxN_\mathcal{E} - 1 \le D_xNE​−1≤Dx​ and a forecast of full rank, Rt=0\mat{R}_t = \mat{0}Rt​=0, the cross terms vanish, and the two smoothers differ only by a rotation, as the docstring says. With NE−1>DxN_\mathcal{E} - 1 > D_xNE​−1>Dx​ they do not vanish in general, and the covariances differ. Program 10.4 measures both regimes.

Fixed-lag smoothing¶

The full pass lets arbitrarily old states feel arbitrarily new data. FixedLagSmoother(lag=L) restarts (10.6) for each anchor sss, from the analysis at min⁡(T,s+L)\min(T, s + L)min(T,s+L) back to sss, and keeps only the result at sss. With L=0L = 0L=0 it is the filter, and with L≥T−1L \ge T - 1L≥T−1 it is EnKS. The batch sweep costs TLT LTL backward steps. The class offers that batch form only: in a streaming setting you hold the last L+1L + 1L+1 ensembles yourself and call smooth on that window.

IES: Gauss-Newton on one window¶

The iterative ensemble smoother Chen & Oliver, 2013Evensen et al., 2019 has no backward pass and no time index. It treats one window as an inverse problem, y=h(θ)+ε\vect{y} = h(\gvect{\theta}) + \gvect{\varepsilon}y=h(θ)+ε, where hhh maps parameters, or an initial state, to the whole observation record. The notation is that of chapter 9: Θ(i)∈RNE×Dθ\gmat{\Theta}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_\theta}Θ(i)∈RNE​×Dθ​ is the iterate, and H~(i)\tilde{\mat{H}}^{(i)}H~(i) holds the anomalies of its image.

Each member draws one perturbed observation, y(e)=y+ε(e)\vect{y}^{(e)} = \vect{y} + \gvect{\varepsilon}^{(e)}y(e)=y+ε(e), and keeps it throughout, so that it minimises one fixed objective,

J(e)(θ)=12∥y(e)−h(θ)∥Σε−12+12∥θ−θ(e,0)∥(Σ^θ(0))−12,\mathcal{J}^{(e)}(\gvect{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2} \Vert \vect{y}^{(e)} - h(\gvect{\theta}) \Vert^2_{\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}} + \frac{1}{2} \Vert \gvect{\theta} - \gvect{\theta}^{(e,0)} \Vert^2_{(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{(0)})^{-1}},J(e)(θ)=21​∥y(e)−h(θ)∥Σε−1​2​+21​∥θ−θ(e,0)∥(Σ^θ(0)​)−12​,
(10.10)

with Σ^θ(0)\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{(0)}Σ^θ(0)​ the covariance of the initial ensemble. Linearising hhh about the current iterate, with a Jacobian J^(i)∈RDy×Dθ\hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_\theta}J^(i)∈RDy​×Dθ​, makes this a linear least-squares problem whose Kalman-form solution is the Gauss-Newton target:

θ(e,i+1)=(1−α)θ(e,i)+α[θ(e,0)+G^(i)(y(e)−h(θ(e,i))+J^(i)(θ(e,i)−θ(e,0)))],\gvect{\theta}^{(e,i+1)} = (1 - \alpha) \gvect{\theta}^{(e,i)} + \alpha \left[\gvect{\theta}^{(e,0)} + \hat{\mat{G}}^{(i)} \left(\vect{y}^{(e)} - h(\gvect{\theta}^{(e,i)}) + \hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)} (\gvect{\theta}^{(e,i)} - \gvect{\theta}^{(e,0)})\right)\right],θ(e,i+1)=(1−α)θ(e,i)+α[θ(e,0)+G^(i)(y(e)−h(θ(e,i))+J^(i)(θ(e,i)−θ(e,0)))],
(10.11)
G^(i)=Σ^θ(0)J^(i)⊤(J^(i)Σ^θ(0)J^(i)⊤+Σε)−1.\hat{\mat{G}}^{(i)} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{(0)} \hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)\top} \left(\hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_\theta^{(0)} \hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)\top} + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon\right)^{-1}.G^(i)=Σ^θ(0)​J^(i)⊤(J^(i)Σ^θ(0)​J^(i)⊤+Σε​)−1.
(10.12)

J^(i)\hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)}J^(i) is the ensemble-average sensitivity, the least-squares fit H~(i)=Θ~(i)J^(i)⊤\tilde{\mat{H}}^{(i)} = \tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^{(i)} \hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)\top}H~(i)=Θ~(i)J^(i)⊤, so J^(i)⊤=(Θ~(i))+H~(i)\hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)\top} = (\tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^{(i)})^{+} \tilde{\mat{H}}^{(i)}J^(i)⊤=(Θ~(i))+H~(i). Only its products with rows of parameters are needed, so everything goes through the NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​ matrix Θ~(0)(Θ~(i))+\tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^{(0)} (\tilde{\gmat{\Theta}}^{(i)})^{+}Θ~(0)(Θ~(i))+, and no Dθ×DθD_\theta \times D_\thetaDθ​×Dθ​ matrix is formed. The damping α∈(0,1]\alpha \in (0, 1]α∈(0,1] is the step_size argument, in the Levenberg-Marquardt style.

The anchor to θ(e,0)\gvect{\theta}^{(e,0)}θ(e,0) separates this from EKI, which drifts from its current iterate and has no memory of where it began. For a linear hhh the term in J^(i)\hat{\mat{J}}^{(i)}J^(i) cancels the change in h(θ(e,i))h(\gvect{\theta}^{(e,i)})h(θ(e,i)), so the bracket is the same at every iteration. With α=1\alpha = 1α=1 the first iterate is then the stochastic ensemble smoother, and later iterates stay there. With α<1\alpha < 1α<1 the distance to it falls by exactly 1−α1 - \alpha1−α per iteration.

Implementation in filterax¶

The backward smoothers take stacked histories of shape (T,NE,Dx)(T, N_\mathcal{E}, D_x)(T,NE​,Dx​), from the Layer 2 assimilate of any filter (chapter 16) or from a loop of your own. They return a SmoothingResult, whose smoothed_history has the same shape. Its particles is the final window, so a smoother chains into a forecast as a filter does.

ClassMethodTakesNote
EnKS, EnsembleRTSsmooththe two histories(10.6), one backward pass
FixedLagSmoother(lag)smooththe two historiesone backward pass per anchor
EnsembleSqrtSmoothersmooththe two histories(10.8), through an eigh of X~X~⊤\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\topX~X~⊤
IES(n_iterations, step_size)solvean initial ensemble, y\vect{y}y, Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ and hhhreturns an AnalysisResult

A Layer 2 filter runs a deterministic dynamics, so its forecasts have no process noise, and (10.7) applies when F\mat{F}F is linear and invertible. A post-analysis inflator does not change that, because the next forecast still propagates the stored analysis, which Program 10.9 checks with RTPS. To carry process noise into the forecast, write the loop yourself around a Layer 1 filter, as Program 10.3 does.

The example uses the model of Program 10.3 with Dx=4D_x = 4Dx​=4 and two observed components, over four windows with 30 members.

It prints (4, 30, 4) and True, so the final window is untouched. It then prints [0.768 0.69 0.612 0.532] [0.637 0.599 0.565 0.532], the spread of the filter and of EnKS in each window. The last line is True, so EnsembleRTS gives the same arrays as EnKS. This short run has no process noise, so the smoothed spread is the final analysis spread grown backward through F−1\mat{F}^{-1}F−1, by (10.7).

Algorithm¶

Program 10.2 writes out the step in both forms, as a dense numpy reference with a square gain and with the pseudo-inverse of (10.6).

It prints True three times: both forms match gaussx, and gaussx matches the second window of the backward pass above.

Agreement with the exact smoother¶

The toy model is the one in tests/test_smoother_workflows.py. It runs the F\mat{F}F above over T=40T = 40T=40 windows, with Ση=0.1I\gmat{\Sigma}_\eta = 0.1 \mat{I}Ση​=0.1I in the truth and in each forecast, and with 100 members. It is linear and Gaussian, so gaussx.kalman_filter and gaussx.rts_smoother give the exact answer. Squared errors are taken on the mean, and they leave out the final window, where every smoother is the analysis.

It prints:

EnKS over the filter, draw by draw[0.668 0.852 0.849]
Exact RTS over the exact filter, draw by draw[0.677 0.821 0.915]
Exact RTS over the exact filter, tr(Σx,t∣T)/tr(Σx,t∣t)\op{tr}(\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid T}) / \op{tr}(\gmat{\Sigma}_{x,t \mid t})tr(Σx,t∣T​)/tr(Σx,t∣t​) at the middle window0.68

So EnKS with 100 members brings the squared error to about 0.78 of the filter’s. The exact smoother’s expected improvement is the variance ratio, 0.68, and the test file compares against that number. The two are not the same kind of quantity, and it would be wrong to read the gap of 0.1 as the cost of using an ensemble. On these same three draws the exact smoother’s own squared-error ratio is 0.79, and the draw-by-draw spread of either is wider than the gap. What three draws can say is that EnKS matches the exact smoother about as closely as they can resolve. The square-root smoother prints the same number because its mean is the same.

The square-root smoother against EnKS¶

Program 10.4 checks the mean, then (10.4) at every window of the first draw, then repeats with fewer members than components.

It prints:

CaseMean gapCovariance gap, first windowMember gap, first windowEnKS from the recursionSquare root from the recursion
NE=100N_\mathcal{E} = 100NE​=100, Dx=4D_x = 4Dx​=42e-155e-020.854e-022e-15
NE=10N_\mathcal{E} = 10NE​=10, Dx=20D_x = 20Dx​=201e-143e-150.233e-153e-15

The means agree in both cases. With NE<DxN_\mathcal{E} < D_xNE​<Dx​ the covariances agree too, and the members differ, so the two really do differ by a rotation. With NE>DxN_\mathcal{E} > D_xNE​>Dx​ the covariances differ by up to 0.05, and only the square-root smoother satisfies (10.4), through the cross terms of (10.9). The EnsembleSqrtSmoother docstring claims a rotation for all finite ensembles, which this case contradicts.

The fixed-lag smoother¶

It prints 1 0.897, 3 0.802, 10 0.754 and 39 0.776, then True True: a lag of 0 returns the filter, and a lag of 39 returns EnKS. Most of the gain arrives in the first few lags. Lag 10 comes out below the full pass, but the draw-by-draw spread above is wider than that difference, so this run does not show that long lags hurt.

IES¶

Program 10.6 first takes the linear problem of chapter 9, whose reference is a stochastic update with the same perturbed observations. It then takes that chapter’s nonlinear model (9.22), with the mean of each member’s objective (10.10) as the measure of progress.

The linear part prints 1.0 1 8.9e-15 and 1.0 5 5.8e-15, so the first iterate is the stochastic update and later ones stay there. With α=0.5\alpha = 0.5α=0.5 it prints 3.3e+00, 1.6e+00 and 2.5e-02 after 1, 2 and 8 iterations, which halves at each iteration as the formula says.

The nonlinear part starts from a mean cost of 26.212, and then prints:

IterationsMean costEnsemble mean
15.896[ 0.7008 -0.6762]
22.590[ 0.8343 -0.6145]
32.256[ 0.8506 -0.5931]
52.238[ 0.8603 -0.5817]
102.239[ 0.8603 -0.5813]

One iteration, the plain ensemble smoother, leaves the mean far from the posterior mean of [ 0.8699 -0.5688] found on the grid in Program 9.10. Five iterations take it within 0.013, at a cost of 1000 evaluations of hhh. The cost then settles rather than falling further, because the ensemble-average sensitivity is not each member’s own Jacobian.

Numerics: float32 and gradients¶

The singular values of the forecast anomalies are the point of the step. A direction 10-4 of the largest has a squared singular value of 10-8 relative, which is below float32’s epsilon, so X~X~⊤\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\topX~X~⊤ cannot hold it. The anomalies themselves can. gaussx.ensemble_rts_step works from them, while EnsembleSqrtSmoother still goes through eigh of the product, with a cutoff at NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ times the epsilon relative to the largest eigenvalue. Program 10.7 builds a forecast with exactly this spread of scales, and moves the smoothed ensemble a little along a weak direction. It then compares each smoother in float32 with its own float64 result.

It prints EnKS 5.0e-08 0.00010794 0.00010789 and sqrt 7.4e-05 0.00010794 0.00003438: the largest gap in the mean, then the mean’s weak component in float64 and in float32. The EnKS step keeps that component to four digits in float32. The square-root smoother returns about a third of it, because its cutoff has dropped the direction. In float64 the two routes agree, so this limit only shows in float32 with a wide spread of scales.

The derivative of the pseudo-inverse has the closed form of Golub & Pereyra (1973), which divides by no difference of singular values. So EnKS keeps finite gradients where singular values repeat or vanish. It holds while the rank is fixed, and a singular value crossing the cutoff changes Xt∣T\mat{X}_{t \mid T}Xt∣T​ discontinuously. EnsembleSqrtSmoother differentiates eigh instead, whose rule divides by the gaps (chapter 6). With NE−1>DxN_\mathcal{E} - 1 > D_xNE​−1>Dx​, the matrix X~X~⊤\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\topX~X~⊤ has a repeated zero eigenvalue. With NE≤DxN_\mathcal{E} \le D_xNE​≤Dx​ that matrix is fine, but after an ETKF with few observations Ψ\gmat{\Psi}Ψ has a repeated eigenvalue of 1.

It prints EnKS, N_E > D_x -2120.743 -2120.743, sqrt, N_E > D_x nan -2122.005 and sqrt, N_E < D_x -1092.115 -1098.199. So EnKS agrees with the central difference, and the square-root smoother gives NaN in the first case and a silently wrong value, off by 0.6%, in the second. Do not train through EnsembleSqrtSmoother.

When it breaks¶

A forecast with no process noise against a truth that has some. Program 10.9 filters the toy model with no noise in the forecast, on the same observation model, for a truth with and without process noise. It checks (10.7), both per window and across the whole run, and then prints the errors.

It prints 1.0847 23.8, the largest growth of F−1\mat{F}^{-1}F−1 per step and over the 39 steps of the run, and then:

TruthGap per window, over the runFilter errorSmoother errorRatioFirst window, filter by drawFirst window, smoother by draw
Ση=0.1I\gmat{\Sigma}_\eta = 0.1 \mat{I}Ση​=0.1I4e-15, 1e-140.3030.3791.25[1.352 0.549 0.741][0.069 0.99 3.498]
Ση=0\gmat{\Sigma}_\eta = \mat{0}Ση​=03e-15, 7e-150.0730.0090.13[1.422 0.463 0.306][0.046 0.085 0.018]

and a last line of 4e-16 for the same identity under RTPS.

The gaps show that (10.7) holds to rounding, so the explanation of the first row is a measured one and not an interpretation. The smoothed run is the final analysis pulled back through F−1\mat{F}^{-1}F−1, which grows the error of that analysis, and it cannot express any process noise the truth had. So the smoother is 25% worse than the filter overall. Early in the run it can be far worse, by a factor of 4.7 in the first window of the third draw, though it is better in the first draw. The second row uses the same smoother and the same algebra on a truth that really has no noise, and the error falls to 0.13 of the filter’s. So the failure belongs to the mismatch between the forecast and the truth, not to the smoother. With process noise back in the forecast, X~t+1∣t\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}X~t+1∣t​ no longer equals X~t∣tF⊤\tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} \mat{F}^\topX~t∣t​F⊤, the identity no longer holds, and the ratio returns to the 0.78 of Program 10.3.

Too few members. With a small ensemble the smoother can do worse than the filter. Program 10.10 also breaks the member correspondence on purpose. The reason I would give is sampling error in the gain, applied again at every window, but that is an interpretation, and the block only measures the outcome.

It prints 5 1.389, 10 1.041 and 20 0.868, then 1.008 for the shuffled case. With Dx=4D_x = 4Dx​=4, 5 members make the smoother 39% worse than the filter, 10 members leave it about even, and 20 start to pay. Shuffling the forecast against the analysis destroys the regression, and the improvement of Program 10.3 disappears.

Two other limits are worth knowing:

  • The final window is never improved, so evaluate a smoother away from the end of the run.

  • The backward step assumes the member correspondence through every stored window. Anything that reorders or resamples members between the stored analysis and the stored forecast breaks it silently, as the shuffled case shows.

When a smoother is the right answer¶

Use EnKS for a reanalysis: one backward pass over a stored history. It needs a forecast with process noise, or a model you trust as exact, and an ensemble large enough to estimate the gain. Use EnsembleRTS for the same run when the RTS reading is the one your code means.

Use EnsembleSqrtSmoother if you need the sample covariance to obey the RTS recursion exactly, with NE>DxN_\mathcal{E} > D_xNE​>Dx​, and you are not differentiating through it. Use FixedLagSmoother when memory or latency bounds how far back you can go. Use IES when one window maps through a strongly nonlinear hhh and you want each member to solve its own objective. History matching is the usual case.

If the forecast is deterministic and the model is exact, the smoother is doing strong-constraint estimation, and the ratio of 0.13 above shows it does that well. If the forecast is deterministic and the model is not exact, add process noise to the forecast before you smooth.
